claim: CRISPR-Cas systems function as defense systems against invading foreign nucleic acids such as bacteriophages and plasmids.
source: CRISPR-Cas systems, encoded in the genomes of many bacterial and archaeal species, function as defense systems against invading foreign nucleic acids such as bacteriophages and plasmids (Barrangou et al., 2007; reviewed in Mohanraju et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barrangou et al., 2007 and Mohanraju et al., 2016, which are referenced as sources of this information.

claim: CRISPR-Cas systems provide acquired immunity by extracting short stretches of foreign nucleic acid and archiving these DNA segments at the CRISPR locus.
source: They provide acquired immunity in which the first step in thwarting an attack involves extracting short stretches of the foreign nucleic acid and archiving these DNA segments (or 'spacers') at the CRISPR locus where they alternate with host-specific repeats; this part of the process is known as adaptation (reviewed in Marraffini, 2015; Sternberg et al., 2016; Amitai and Sorek, 2016; Jackson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple review citations (Marraffini, 2015; Sternberg et al., 2016; Amitai and Sorek, 2016; Jackson et al., 2017).

claim: The CRISPR locus is transcribed as a long CRISPR RNA (pre-crRNA) that is digested into shorter pieces (crRNAs).
source: The CRISPR locus is then transcribed as a long CRISPR RNA (pre-crRNA) that is digested into shorter pieces (crRNAs).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas systems, presented as part of the background information.

claim: Guide crRNAs are incorporated into a ribonucleoprotein interference complex that can recognize and cleave its complementary target sequence.
source: These 'guide' crRNAs are incorporated into a ribonucleoprotein interference complex that can recognize and cleave its complementary target sequence, thus destroying the invading nucleic acid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: Cas1 protein is common to all known autonomous CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: Common to all known autonomous CRISPR-Cas systems is the Cas1 protein (Makarova et al., 2013; Makarova et al., 2018; Wright et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Makarova et al., 2013, 2018 and Wright et al., 2019.

claim: Cas1 acts in concert with Cas2 to recognize, process, and integrate protospacers into the CRISPR-Cas locus.
source: which acts in concert with its binding partner Cas2 to recognize, process, and integrate protospacers into the CRISPR-Cas locus (Yosef et al., 2012; Nuñez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yosef et al., 2012 and Nuñez et al., 2014.

claim: Type V-C and V-D CRISPR-Cas systems lack a cas2 gene.
source: Notable exceptions are the type V-C and V-D systems which lack a cas2 gene (Shmakov et al., 2015; Burstein et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shmakov et al., 2015 and Burstein et al., 2017.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis suggests that Cas1 proteins may have originated from casposons.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of Cas1 proteins suggests that they may have originated from casposons, a novel class of putative DNA transposons in which a Cas1 homolog (the 'casposase') functions as the transposase (Figure 1A; Krupovic et al., 2014; Koonin and Makarova, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Krupovic et al., 2014 and Koonin and Makarova, 2017, and references Figure 1A.

claim: The evolution of CRISPR-Cas systems would parallel that of the adaptive immune system in higher eukaryotes, which evolved from an ancient DNA transposon.
source: If so, the evolution of CRISPR-Cas systems would parallel that of the adaptive immune system in higher eukaryotes, which evolved from an ancient DNA transposon (Kapitonov and Jurka, 2005; Carmona and Schatz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is conditional ('If so') and supported by citations to Kapitonov and Jurka, 2005 and Carmona and Schatz, 2017.

claim: The active Cas1-Cas2 integrase is an elongated (Cas1)2(Cas2)2(Cas1)2 heterohexamer.
source: The active integrase is an elongated (Cas1)2(Cas2)2(Cas1)2 heterohexamer in which two catalytic Cas1 monomers carry out metal-dependent transesterification to integrate protospacers into the target repeat sequence (Yosef et al., 2012; Nuñez et al., 2014; Nuñez et al., 2015a; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Wang et al., 2015; Rollie et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Yosef et al., 2012; Nuñez et al., 2014; Nuñez et al., 2015a; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Wang et al., 2015; Rollie et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017).

claim: Efficient protospacer integration requires 3'-single stranded overhangs on each spacer end.
source: Efficient protospacer integration requires 3'-single stranded overhangs on each spacer end, and integration of the two 3'-ends into opposing strands of the target leads to the duplication of the CRISPR repeat.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas integration mechanisms.

claim: The casposase from Aciduliprofundum boonei is an active DNA integrase in vitro.
source: Although the casposase from the archaeon Aciduliprofundum boonei is an active DNA integrase in vitro (Hickman and Dyda, 2015; Béguin et al., 2016; Béguin et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hickman and Dyda, 2015; Béguin et al., 2016; Béguin et al., 2019.

claim: In vivo transposition activity of casposases has yet to be demonstrated.
source: in vivo transposition activity has yet to be demonstrated
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding casposases.

claim: Only the casposase and a family B polymerase appear common to all casposons.
source: Casposons contain varying collections of other genes (as shown schematically in Figure 1A), but only the casposase and a family B polymerase appear common to all (Krupovic et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krupovic et al., 2017 and references Figure 1A.

claim: The M. mazei casposase can integrate varied forms of the casposon end in vitro.
source: We show here that the Methanosarcina mazei casposase can integrate varied forms of the casposon end in vitro
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The M. mazei casposase recapitulates several properties of CRISPR-Cas integrases including site-specificity.
source: and recapitulates several properties of CRISPR-Cas integrases including site-specificity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The X-ray structure of the casposase bound to DNA reveals a tetramer with target DNA bound snugly between two dimers.
source: The X-ray structure of the casposase bound to DNA representing the product of integration reveals a tetramer with target DNA bound snugly between two dimers in which single-stranded casposon end binding resembles that of spacer 3'-overhangs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural data.

claim: Single-stranded casposon end binding in the casposase structure resembles that of spacer 3'-overhangs.
source: The X-ray structure of the casposase bound to DNA representing the product of integration reveals a tetramer with target DNA bound snugly between two dimers in which single-stranded casposon end binding resembles that of spacer 3'-overhangs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural data.

claim: The differences between transposase and CRISPR-Cas integrase are largely architectural.
source: The differences between transposase and CRISPR-Cas integrase are largely architectural
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: Evolutionary change from casposase to CRISPR-Cas integrase involved changes in protein-protein interactions to favor Cas2 binding over tetramerization.
source: and it appears that evolutionary change involved changes in protein-protein interactions to favor Cas2 binding over tetramerization; this in turn led to preferred integration of single spacers over two transposon ends.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A large family of closely related casposons are present in multiple strains of Methanosarcina mazei.
source: Recently it was reported that a large family of closely related casposons are present in multiple strains of Methanosarsina mazei (Krupovic et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krupovic et al., 2016.

claim: Different strains of M. mazei have casposons in different genomic locations.
source: Different strains of M. mazei have casposons in different genomic locations, strongly suggesting that these casposons are either currently active or have recently been active.
evidence: This is an observation that leads to an inference about casposon activity.

claim: One commonly observed genomic location for casposons in M. mazei is within tRNA-Leu genes.
source: One commonly observed genomic location for casposons in this species is within tRNA-Leu genes.
evidence: This is an observation about casposon genomic locations.

claim: There is a short consensus sequence, 5'-CGCA, within the TSDs observed in vivo for M. mazei casposons.
source: Analysis of integration sites suggested that there is a short consensus sequence, 5'-CGCA, within the TSDs observed in vivo (Krupovic et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krupovic et al., 2016.

claim: The M. mazei casposase produces relaxed and linear products consistent with single-ended and double-ended integrations when the specific target plasmid pUC19+TSD+30 bp is used.
source: relaxed products consistent with single-ended integration (SE) and linear products consistent with double-ended (DE) integration were readily observed when the TSD+30 bp of the tRNA-Leu gene were included (lanes 16–20).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Integration by the M. mazei casposase is target-specific.
source: These results suggested that integration by the M. mazei casposase is target-specific, and that the target site is contained within the sequence corresponding to TSD+30 bp.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The casposase differentiates between the available 3'-OH groups of supplied oligonucleotides, and uses only the 3'-OH group at the casposon end as the nucleophile for integration.
source: These results indicate that the casposase differentiates between the available 3'-OH groups of supplied oligonucleotides, and uses only the 3'-OH group at the casposon end as the nucleophile for integration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The M. mazei casposase has a wide tolerance for the type and sequence of oligonucleotides it can integrate.
source: the results indicate that the M. mazei casposase has a wide tolerance for the type and sequence of oligonucleotides it can integrate, but with an apparent preference for a partially single-stranded casposon end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The M. mazei casposase has an apparent preference for a partially single-stranded casposon end.
source: the results indicate that the M. mazei casposase has a wide tolerance for the type and sequence of oligonucleotides it can integrate, but with an apparent preference for a partially single-stranded casposon end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Casposon ends as short as six nucleotides can be specifically integrated by the M. mazei casposase.
source: Remarkably, casposon ends as short as six nt could be specifically integrated, a result that has also recently been demonstrated for the A. boonei casposase (Béguin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and by citation to Béguin et al., 2019.

claim: Integration occurred overwhelmingly and with precision into the specific target site of pUC19+TSD+30 bp (designated target site one or TS1).
source: The results reveal that integration occurred overwhelmingly and with precision into the specific target site of pUC19+TSD+30 bp (designated target site one or TS1), with sequences from all five samples revealing overlapping positive and negative strand insertions consistent with the 14 bp offset corresponding to the size of casposon TSDs (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by NGS data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: For sample S5D, 99.4% of the detected integration events were at TS1.
source: For sample S5D, 99.4% of the detected integration events were at TS1
evidence: This is a quantitative result from NGS analysis.

claim: No sequences were detected that would have been generated if the opposite 3'-end of the casposon end oligonucleotides were used as the nucleophile.
source: We detected no sequences that would have been generated if the opposite 3'-end of the casposon end oligonucleotides were used as the nucleophile.
evidence: This is a result from NGS analysis.

claim: Integration by the M. mazei casposase is remarkably sequence-specific.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that integration by the M. mazei casposase is remarkably sequence-specific
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NGS data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The most important target sequence features directing integration are clustered around the 5'-CGCA motif.
source: and that the most important target sequence features directing integration are clustered around the 5'-CGCA motif detected in vivo (Krupovic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NGS data and supported by citation to Krupovic et al., 2016.

claim: The conserved 5'-CGCA target motif is critical for integration.
source: The conserved 5'-CGCA target motif was critical as its mutation resulted in almost complete loss of both top and bottom strand integration ('mutCGCA').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutation of four bp just 5' of the CGCA motif severely reduced integration.
source: Mutation of four bp just 5' of the CGCA motif ('mutL') severely reduced integration
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutating the last five bp of the TSD reduced integration, although to a lesser extent than mutating the region 5' of CGCA.
source: as did mutating the last five bp of the TSD ('mutR'), although to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutation of the region corresponding to bp 12–17 abolished casposase activity.
source: we mutated the region corresponding to bp 12–17, and this abolished activity ('mut12-17').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Symmetrizing the TSD was as effective a target as the original TSD.
source: We were also curious how symmetrizing the TSD (i.e., placing the 5'-CGCA motif on both strands at the target site) might impact activity and we found it was as effective a target as the original TSD ('symTSD').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Maximal activity for bottom strand integration was obtained once the 3'-overhang was 2-nt.
source: Maximal activity for bottom strand integration was obtained once the 3'-overhang was 2-nt and was thereafter essentially unchanged as the length of the overhang was increased to 7-nt.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Integration into the top strand as a function of 3'-overhang length lagged behind that of bottom strand integration.
source: Integration into the top strand as a function of 3'-overhang length lagged behind that of bottom strand integration, and reached its maximal level once the 3'-overhang was 4-nt.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Only a few unpaired nucleotides are required at the casposon end for optimal integration activity.
source: these results suggest that only a few unpaired nucleotides are required at the casposon end for optimal integration activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: ssRNA can be integrated by the M. mazei casposase.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, ssRNA also can be integrated into the target oligonucleotide targ40 although far less efficiently.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At low protein concentrations used for iSCAMS, the M. mazei casposase had a measured MW of 95 kDa, consistent with a dimer.
source: At the low protein concentrations used for iSCAMS (25–50 nM), the M. mazei casposase had a measured MW of 95 kDa (Figure 4), consistent with a dimer
evidence: This is supported by iSCAMS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the presence of a 17-nt ssDNA casposon end (ssLE17), the MW of the casposase shifted to 109 kDa, suggesting binding while the protein remained dimeric.
source: In the presence of a 17-nt ssDNA casposon end (ssLE17), the MW shifted to 109 kDa, suggesting binding while the protein remained dimeric.
evidence: This is supported by iSCAMS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the presence of a branched oligonucleotide substrate representing the integration product, the resulting protein-DNA complex had a measured MW of 219 kDa, consistent with a tetramer bound to one integration product molecule.
source: In the presence of a branched oligonucleotide substrate comprised of two single-stranded 8-nt casposon ends linked to a symmetrized target sequence mimicking the integration product (minus any overhangs that might be present in vivo), the resulting protein-DNA complex had a measured MW of 219 kDa, consistent with a tetramer bound to one integration product molecule.
evidence: This is supported by iSCAMS data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When the casposase was titrated with either TR17 or ssLE17, the casposase bound with a stoichiometry of one end per dimer.
source: When the casposase was titrated with either TR17 or ssLE17, the casposase bound with a stoichiometry of one end per dimer (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elution position of the casposase varied as a function of concentration.
source: During the course of these experiments, it became clear that the elution position of the casposase varied as a function of concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The casposase exhibits a concentration-dependent equilibrium between dimeric and tetrameric forms.
source: Thus, it appears that the casposase exhibits a concentration-dependent equilibrium between dimeric and tetrameric forms, and that this equilibrium is affected upon binding to DNA substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from SEC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structure of the casposase-DNA complex was solved to 3.1 Å using experimental phases obtained from a selenomethionine derivative.
source: the structure of the complex was solved to 3.1 Å using experimental phases obtained from a selenomethionine derivative (Table 1; Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Table 1, Figure 5, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The casposase-DNA complex is a clamp-like tetramer in which two casposase dimers hold the double-stranded target site between them.
source: The pseudo two-fold symmetric complex is a clamp-like tetramer in which two casposase dimers hold the double-stranded target site between them, with the 5' termini of the single-stranded casposon ends emerging through a narrow slot in the bottom of the clamp (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Each casposase monomer exhibits the fold expected of a Cas1 homolog.
source: Each casposase monomer exhibits the fold expected of a Cas1 homolog (Wiedenheft et al., 2009; Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3)
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3, and by citation to Wiedenheft et al., 2009.

claim: The casposase has a canonical eight-stranded N-terminal domain and a globular catalytic domain.
source: with a canonical eight-stranded N-terminal domain and a globular catalytic domain that brings conserved active site residues (E162, H232, E247) into close proximity (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The N-terminal domains of the casposase and A. fulgidus Cas1 have an RMSD of 1.68 Å over 72 shared Cα positions.
source: When compared to its most closely related structurally characterized Cas1 homolog, that from Archaeoglobus fulgidus (Kim et al., 2013) with which it shares 32% sequence identity, the N-terminal domains have an RMSD of 1.68 Å over 72 shared Cα positions
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claim: The catalytic domains of the casposase and A. fulgidus Cas1 have an RMSD of 1.28 Å over 208 shared Cα positions.
source: and the catalytic domains are even more similar, with an RMSD of 1.28 Å over 208 shared Cα positions.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: In the integration product complex, each dimer is functionally and structurally asymmetric with a 'catalytic' monomer and a 'noncatalytic' monomer.
source: In the integration product complex, each dimer is functionally and structurally asymmetric with a 'catalytic' monomer whose active site contains the scissile phosphate group that links transposon end DNA and the target site, and a 'noncatalytic' monomer in which the active site is located on the periphery of the assembly facing away from the DNA.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The functional asymmetry at the dimer level recapitulates the observed asymmetry of Cas1 dimers in structurally characterized CRISPR Cas1-Cas2 integration complexes bound to DNA.
source: This functional asymmetry at the dimer level recapitulates the observed asymmetry of Cas1 dimers in structurally characterized CRISPR Cas1-Cas2 integration complexes bound to DNA (Nuñez et al., 2015b; Wang et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to known structures, supported by citations to Nuñez et al., 2015b; Wang et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017.

claim: There is interpretable density for all four monomers until amino acid 341, but thereafter the C-terminus is not visible in two of the monomers.
source: In the complex, there is interpretable density for all four monomers until amino acid 341, but thereafter the C-terminus is not visible in two of the monomers and, in the other two, there is interpretable density only until residues 354 and 359.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The C-terminal residues remain disordered within the crystal when the casposase is bound to the integration product mimic.
source: Thus it appears that when the casposase is bound to this integration product mimic, the C-terminal residues remain disordered within the crystal and do not stably engage with the rest of the protein or DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural data and additional experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The C-terminally truncated casposase (ΔHTH) has no evidence of integration activity with any integration substrates.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, there was no evidence of integration activity with any of our integration substrates, using either the specific pUC19+TSD+30 bp target or on pUC19 alone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The casposase N-terminal and catalytic domains alone are not sufficient for integration.
source: Thus, the casposase N-terminal and catalytic domains alone are not sufficient for integration, and the HTH domain must play a crucial role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Two dimer-to-dimer interactions are formed by the convergence of helix α1 and a loop from each noncatalytic monomer with two loops from the opposing catalytic monomer.
source: In the tetrameric complex with the integration product DNA, we observe two dimer-to-dimer interactions (Figure 6C) formed by the convergence of helix α1 (residues 59–67) and a loop (residues 39–44 between β4 and β5) from each noncatalytic monomer with two loops (residues 182–199 and 275–278) from the opposing catalytic monomer.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Each set of dimer-to-dimer interactions buries a surface area of ~1200 Å in the tetramerization interface.
source: Each set of interactions buries a surface area of ~1200 Å in the tetramerization interface and together form the base of the clamp in which the dsDNA target is enclosed.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from structural analysis.

claim: The M. mazei casposase generates 14 bp TSDs.
source: The M. mazei casposase generates 14 bp TSDs (Figure 3A–C)
evidence: This is supported by NGS data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: CRISPR repeats that are the TSDs are generally 25–50 bp.
source: in sharp contrast to CRISPR-Cas systems where the CRISPR repeats that are the TSDs (generated after spacer integration and subsequent repair by DNA replication) are generally 25–50 bp.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: Both Cas1 and Cas2 participate in binding the CRISPR repeat in CRISPR-Cas integrases.
source: In the case of CRISPR-Cas integrases, both Cas1 and Cas2 participate in binding the CRISPR repeat (Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2017 and Wright et al., 2017.

claim: The total casposase-dsDNA interface buries ~4700 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface.
source: In the casposase complex structure, the total casposase-dsDNA interface buries ~4700 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface
evidence: This is a quantitative result from structural analysis.

claim: Only two specific contacts mediate the interaction between the casposase and target DNA: between R191 and G22, and between R192 and G20.
source: but only two specific contacts mediate the interaction with the target DNA: between R191 and G22 (i.e., the base opposite the first C of the 5'-CGCA motif) and between R192 and G20 (the base opposite the second C of the 5'-CGCA motif) (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: The bound target in the integration product complex is almost perfectly straight B-form DNA.
source: The bound target in the integration product complex is almost perfectly straight B-form DNA, unlike the severely bent targets observed in other DNA transpososomes and retroviral intasomes (for example, Montaño et al., 2012; Maertens et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by comparison to other structures cited (Montaño et al., 2012; Maertens et al., 2010).

claim: The R191A/R192A double mutant had little or no relaxed or linear products observed when TR17 was used.
source: When the optimal oligonucleotide substrate, TR17, was used, there was little or no relaxed or linear products observed (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The R191A/R192A double mutant had little evidence for any activity with a range of different casposon end substrates.
source: We also tested a range of different casposon end substrates, and again there was little evidence for any activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: R191 and R192 play important roles during integration.
source: supporting the notion that these two arginines play important roles during integration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from mutagenesis data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The only base-specific interaction between the casposase and casposon end is between the first C of the casposon DNA (C8) and the side chain of K238.
source: Although the only base-specific interaction is between the first C of the casposon DNA (C8) and the side chain of K238, several residues interact with the phosphate backbone (H232, R250, Y206, R280, and R287) and there are arrays of stacking interactions.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Each single-stranded casposon end buries ~1700 Å total solvent-accessible surface area through extensive interactions.
source: Through these extensive interactions, each single-stranded casposon end buries ~1700 Å total solvent-accessible surface area.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from structural analysis.

claim: The M194A/Y243A, Y206A/R280A, and W77A mutants had severely reduced integration activity when assayed using TR17.
source: Each of these mutants had severely reduced integration activity when assayed using TR17, most notably for the production of the linear product (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: None of the mutant proteins (M194A/Y243A, Y206A/R280A, W77A) generated a linear product consistent with double-ended integration when other casposon end substrates were tested.
source: When other casposon end substrates were tested (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), there were varying levels of residual activity for the production of the relaxed form of the pUC19+TSD+30 bp plasmid (consistent with SE joining), but none of the mutant proteins generated a linear product consistent with double-ended integration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: All of the mutants showed a higher activity level with a casposon-specific ssDNA end (ssLE17) than with non-specific DNA (ssran17).
source: Interestingly, all of the mutants showed a higher activity level with a casposon-specific ssDNA end (ssLE17) than with non-specific DNA (ssran17).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The path followed by ssDNA from the casposase active sites is reminiscent of those of the 3' overhangs of CRISPR spacers.
source: The path followed by ssDNA from the casposase active sites is reminiscent of those of the 3' overhangs of CRISPR spacers (Wang et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017) although the number and type of interactions differ (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a structural comparison supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017, and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Several CRISPR Cas1 proteins have been reported to bind ssDNA.
source: Consistent with the importance of ssDNA overhangs at the end of spacers, several CRISPR Cas1 proteins have been reported to bind ssDNA
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR Cas1 proteins.

claim: Stable half-site integration of single-stranded protospacers has not been detected for most CRISPR Cas1 proteins.
source: and although ssDNA can be disintegrated by Cas1 (Rollie et al., 2015), stable half-site integration of single-stranded protospacers has not been detected (Nuñez et al., 2015b; Fagerlund et al., 2017; Rollie et al., 2018) although an exception has been reported (Silas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rollie et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Fagerlund et al., 2017; Rollie et al., 2018; Silas et al., 2016.

claim: The putative evolution from transposition to spacer integration may have involved the loss of the coupling between ssDNA binding and subsequent integration.
source: These collective observations suggest that the putative evolution from transposition to spacer integration may have involved the loss of the coupling between ssDNA binding and subsequent integration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural and biochemical observations.

claim: The mode of target binding by the casposase resembles that of E. faecalis and E. coli Cas1 bound to CRISPR repeats.
source: As can be seen in Figure 8A, the mode of target binding by the casposase resembles that of E. faecalis and E. coli Cas1 bound to CRISPR repeats
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The binding mode of the ssDNA casposon ends resembles that of 3'-overhangs of CRISPR spacers.
source: and the binding mode of the ssDNA casposon ends resembles that of 3'-overhangs of CRISPR spacers (Wang et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a structural comparison supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2017.

claim: One of the casposase monomers occupies the same architectural space as one of the Cas2 subunits in CRISPR Cas1-Cas2 complexes.
source: However, when the casposase tetramer is considered (Figure 8B), it is clear that one of the casposase monomers occupies the same architectural space as one of the Cas2 subunits in CRISPR Cas1-Cas2 complexes (Figure 8B, center)
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claim: It would not be possible to retain the ability to tetramerize in the manner observed and to simultaneously bind Cas2.
source: and it would not be possible to retain the ability to tetramerize in the manner observed and to simultaneously bind Cas2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claim: At the level of the casposase dimer, there does not appear to be an obvious structural impediment to interacting with a Cas2 dimer.
source: At the level of the casposase dimer, however, there does not appear to be an obvious structural impediment to interacting with a Cas2 dimer (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Mutation of only a few surface residues of the casposase might be sufficient to convert it into one with both a complementary shape and the necessary residues to bind Cas2.
source: Although the specifics of Cas1-Cas2 interactions are not conserved across CRISPR-Cas systems (Wang et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017), when the relevant interfaces were compared, it appears that mutation of only a few surface residues of the casposase might be sufficient to convert it into one with both a complementary shape and the necessary residues to bind Cas2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural comparison, supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015; Nuñez et al., 2015b; Xiao et al., 2017.

claim: The M. mazei casposase already possesses several observed properties of Cas1-Cas2 integrases.
source: Our biochemical results described here indicate that the M. mazei casposase already possesses several observed properties of Cas1-Cas2 integrases (Marraffini, 2015; Sternberg et al., 2016; Amitai and Sorek, 2016; Jackson et al., 2017), as has also been recently reported for the A. boonei casposase (Béguin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from biochemical data presented in the manuscript, supported by citations to Marraffini, 2015; Sternberg et al., 2016; Amitai and Sorek, 2016; Jackson et al., 2017; Béguin et al., 2019.

claim: The crucial identity of a few bp on each side of the top strand casposon integration site corresponds to the conserved feature of CRISPR-Cas integration for specificity to the leader-repeat border.
source: For example, the crucial identity of a few bp on each side of the top strand casposon integration site (Figure 3E, mutCGCA and mutL) corresponds to the conserved feature of CRISPR-Cas integration for specificity to the leader-repeat border.
evidence: This is a comparison between casposase and CRISPR-Cas integration properties, supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Specific integration of a transposon avoids any possible deleterious effects of random integration on the host cell genome.
source: Specific integration of a transposon avoids any possible deleterious effects of random integration on the host cell genome
evidence: This is a general principle about transposon integration.

claim: For CRISPR-Cas, specific integration ensures that the latest encountered cellular invader is effectively neutralized as it generates the most robust immune response.
source: whereas for CRISPR-Cas, this also ensures that the latest encountered cellular invader is effectively neutralized as it generates the most robust immune response (McGinn and Marraffini, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McGinn and Marraffini, 2016.

claim: The requirement for a sequence motif upstream of the casposon integration site appears to correspond to the observation that in some CRISPR-Cas systems, sequences upstream within the leader are important for integration.
source: Furthermore, the requirement for a sequence motif upstream of the casposon integration site (Figures 1B and 3E mut12-17) appears to correspond to the observation that in some CRISPR-Cas systems, sequences upstream within the leader are important for integration (Alkhnbashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison between casposase and CRISPR-Cas integration properties, supported by data shown in Figures 1B and 3E, and by citation to Alkhnbashi et al., 2016.

claim: In the E. coli Type I-E system, IHF binds within the last 40 bp of the leader and is needed to bend and deform the target site so that integration can occur.
source: This requirement is understood for the E. coli Type I-E system in which IHF binds within the last 40 bp of the leader and is needed to bend and deform the target site so that integration can occur (Nuñez et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nuñez et al., 2016 and Wright et al., 2017.

claim: It is possible that the role of the casposase HTH domain is to recognize a specific sequence just upstream of the integration site and thereby direct integration.
source: It is possible that the role of the casposase HTH domain is to recognize a specific sequence just upstream of the integration site and thereby direct integration; this would be consistent with our observation that it is crucial for activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The crucial change in the evolutionary pathway from casposase to CRISPR-Cas integrase was architectural.
source: Based on the biochemistry and structure presented here, we suggest an evolutionary pathway in which the crucial change was architectural (Figure 9B, Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on biochemical and structural data presented in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: The ability of the casposase to tetramerize on DNA upon target binding was lost when it acquired a preference for binding to a Cas2 molecule rather than to itself.
source: In this scenario, the ability of the casposase to tetramerize on DNA upon target binding was lost when it acquired a preference for binding to a Cas2 molecule rather than to itself.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary pathway.

claim: The total protein surface buried by the casposase by tetramerization (~2400 Å2) is substantially smaller than the total Cas1-Cas2 buried surface in the heterohexamer of either E. coli (~7800 Å2) or of E. faecalis (~4000 Å2).
source: This seems a reasonable possibility as the total protein surface buried by the casposase by tetramerization (~2400 Å2) is substantially smaller than the total Cas1-Cas2 buried surface in the heterohexamer of either E. coli (~7800 Å2; Nuñez et al., 2014) or of E. faecalis (~4000 Å2; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supported by citations to Nuñez et al., 2014 and Xiao et al., 2017.

claim: If an intervening Cas2 dimer were introduced as a bridge between the two noncatalytic subunits of the casposase tetramer, the active sites of the catalytic monomers would remain oriented towards each other.
source: As shown by the structure here, if an intervening Cas2 dimer were introduced as a bridge between the two noncatalytic subunits of the casposase tetramer, the active sites of the catalytic monomers would not only remain oriented towards each other but Cas2 would provide an additional DNA binding surface that could preferentially direct a single, short piece of DNA between two active sites.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural data.

claim: In the evolutionary model, the CRISPR repeat sequence would be derived from the original target site preferred by the casposase.
source: In this model, the CRISPR repeat sequence would be therefore derived from the original target site preferred by the casposase, and any original specificity for the casposon terminal inverted repeats would devolve to a residual spacer sequence preference.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary pathway.

claim: The RAG1 protein of the V(D)J recombinase conserves properties of its original transposase in that specific signal sequences are recognized and cleaved out from its flanking coding sequences.
source: We note that the RAG1 protein of the V(D)J recombinase, also derived from a DNA transposon, conserves properties of its original transposase in that specific signal sequences are recognized and cleaved out from its flanking coding sequences (Schatz and Swanson, 2011) while the random integration activity has been severely reduced to avoid genomic damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schatz and Swanson, 2011.

claim: When Cas2 was acquired as a preferred binding partner, it seems likely that Cas1 active sites would be forced farther apart in CRISPR integrases than in casposases, thereby expanding the length of the target site duplication.
source: In the evolutionary model presented here, when Cas2 was acquired as a preferred binding partner, it seems likely that Cas1 active sites would be forced farther apart in CRISPR integrases than in casposases, thereby expanding the length of the target site duplication.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary pathway.

claim: Expanding the length of the target site duplication could have been important to allow the sampling of longer pieces of DNA which would produce more specific crRNA for incorporation into effector complexes.
source: As has been pointed out (Wright et al., 2019), this could have been important to allow the sampling of longer pieces of DNA which would produce more specific crRNA for incorporation into effector complexes at a later step in the immunity process.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Wright et al., 2019.

claim: The presence in M. mazei strains of 'solo-TIRs' of specific length might be evidence of the capacity of a casposase to integrate short spacer-like sequences or an early step along the path to the development of a CRISPR array.
source: Indeed, the presence in M. mazei strains of 'solo-TIRs' of specific length (either 19 or 31 bp; Krupovic et al., 2016) might be evidence of the capacity of a casposase to integrate short spacer-like sequences or an early step along the path to the development of a CRISPR array (Jackson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Krupovic et al., 2016 and Jackson et al., 2017.

claim: A type V-C Cas1 protein is active in vitro for spacer integration in the absence of Cas2.
source: It has recently been reported that a type V-C Cas1 protein is active in vitro for spacer integration in the absence of Cas2, and has been proposed to be an early ancestor of the Cas1-Cas2 spacer acquisition system (Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wright et al., 2019.

claim: The V-C Cas1 forms a tetrameric assembly upon binding to oligonucleotides that represent spacer integration products.
source: Like the casposase here, the V-C Cas1 forms a tetrameric assembly upon binding to oligonucleotides that represent spacer integration products
evidence: This is a comparison to the V-C Cas1 system.

claim: The V-C Cas1 has an exquisite preference for spacers that are recessed by 0–2 nt on one strand.
source: The first is its exquisite preference for spacers that are recessed by 0–2 nt on one strand: spacers that are recessed by three nt or longer are not functional for spacer integration
evidence: This is a property of the V-C Cas1 system.

claim: The 25 bp V-C target site is substantially larger than the ~14 bp average for casposases.
source: The second difference from casposases is the length of the target site as the 25 bp V-C target site, although shorter than average for CRISPR-Cas systems, is substantially larger than the ~14 bp average for casposases (Krupovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison between V-C Cas1 and casposases, supported by citation to Krupovic et al., 2014.

claim: The V-C Cas1 is less sequence-specific in its integration site preference relative to other characterized Cas1-Cas2 integrases.
source: Finally, the V-C Cas1 is less sequence-specific in its integration site preference relative to other characterized Cas1-Cas2 integrases (Wright et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wright et al., 2019.
